prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Bless Tuesday, blessed Monday. Bless the word week, its seven small days trail with y. Bless the men whose words I was too young to hear. A whisper loves a canal. Bless my laugh, lent by grief, I have so little left to borrow. But my hair, it grows— if hair be gold, cut mine so I might rid my beloved of his student loans. Bless thieves, universities, those hands caress what’s not theirs. Bless thinking it was yours. Here are hands, blessed one. Bless them holding the door. Bless each crier on the F train before and after me as they blush, as they transfer into tunnels for the red line. Oh bless, bless wildly, what remains to be done. Bless the one who told me so, the ones who didn’t. Even weak breaths bless. Bless weakness, fragile fortress, my friend’s body absent of soundness. Bless the sound of someone reliable answering your call, saying If you’re going through hell, Hello.

outputs.L2:
**A Blessing, Reimagined**

Sacred be Monday's arrival, sacred Tuesday's turn. Sacred too the very notion of a week—seven modest days, each one ending softly in "y." I offer blessing to those men whose voices reached me before I had ears to understand them. There's a hush that finds itself drawn to waterways.

I bless this laugh of mine, borrowed on credit from sorrow—for I have precious little else to lend against. Yet my hair keeps growing, stubborn as ever; were it truly golden, I'd shear it all off to free the one I love from the weight of his debts.

I bless the universities, those polished thieves, whose grasping hands claim what was never rightfully theirs. I bless the illusion of ownership, the mistaken sense that something belonged to you. Here—take these hands, you who are blessed. I bless the simple act of holding a door open for another.

I bless every weeping stranger I pass on the F train, both ahead of me and behind, their faces flushing as they descend toward the connecting tunnels leading to the red line. Oh, let blessing fall recklessly, extravagantly, upon whatever labor still awaits completion.

I bless the person who spoke truth to me, and equally those who withheld it. Blessing exists even in breath grown thin and faint. I bless frailty itself—that delicate stronghold—and my friend's body, stripped now of its former strength. And I bless that particular sound: a trustworthy voice picking up the phone, saying, *If you're walking through hell right now—hello.*
outputs.L3:
# The Sanctification of the Ordinary: An Analysis of Blessing as Refrain

Throughout the poem, the word "bless" functions as a persistent, almost incantatory refrain, transforming the mundane texture of daily life into something worthy of reverence. The speaker does not reserve this benediction for moments of obvious grace or triumph; instead, blessing extends to weekdays—those unremarkable, repetitive units of time that structure our lives—as well as to personal grief, suggesting that pain itself deserves acknowledgment rather than dismissal. This repetition creates a rhythm that mirrors prayer, elevating the poem's structure to something liturgical, where even suffering becomes a site of sacred attention.

The poem also turns inward toward memory, reflecting on youth as a state of incomplete understanding. The speaker recalls being too young to grasp certain words or experiences that were shared among men—a phrase that suggests both a literal linguistic gap and a broader exclusion from adult knowledge or masculine rites of passage. This admission carries a quiet melancholy, acknowledging that comprehension often arrives too late, after the moment that required it has already passed.

Material and institutional pressures surface as well, particularly through an imagined gesture of sacrifice: the speaker envisions cutting their own hair as a means of relieving a loved one's student debt. This image, both tender and desperate, speaks to the lengths one might imagine going to in order to protect someone else from financial burden. Embedded within this moment is a sharper critique—universities are cast as thieves, institutions that strip students not only of money but of ownership and identity, leaving them indebted in ways that extend beyond the merely economic.

Amid these larger structural concerns, the poem remains deeply attentive to small, fleeting human connections. A stranger crying on a train, a friend's physical frailty—these moments of shared vulnerability are not overlooked but are instead framed as precisely the kind of experience that deserves blessing. In this way, the poem insists that dignity and grace are found not in grand gestures but in the quiet, often unnoticed instances of human fragility witnessed in passing.

The poem ultimately closes on an image of steadfast comfort: a blessing bestowed upon the presence of someone who, when called upon in a moment of need, answers with warmth despite their own hardships. This final gesture consolidates the poem's central preoccupation—that blessing is not reserved for the exceptional, but is most powerfully found in reliability, in the simple act of showing up for another person even amid one's own struggles.
outputs.L4:
# Blessing

Blessed be the ordinary days that ask nothing of us
but to be lived, hour folding into hour
like laundry we forgot we owned.

Blessed be the hair that falls out in fistfuls,
that thins at the temples, that grays
before we are ready—blessed be
the comb that finds it anyway,
patient as a mother.

Blessed be laughter that arrives uninvited
at funerals, at the worst possible moment,
because the body knows what the mind refuses:
that grief and joy share a doorway,
that sometimes you must laugh
or the grief will eat you first.

Blessed be grief itself, unglamorous,
sitting at the kitchen table in its bathrobe,
refusing to leave, teaching us
the weight of what we loved.

Blessed be the thief who takes only
what he needs—the bicycle, the twenty dollars,
the hour of sleep—for even in taking
he is asking, in his broken language,
to be seen, to be forgiven,
to be more than the hand that grabs.

Blessed be the debt we carry,
the interest that accrues like guilt,
because it means someone trusted us
enough to let us owe them.

Blessed be the riders on the 6 train,
the woman with three children and one seat,
the man who gives it up without being asked,
the boy asleep against a stranger's shoulder,
all of us borrowed toward the same station,
all of us willing, for a moment, to be gentle
with people we will never see again.

Blessed be the body, this fragile
arrangement of water and calcium,
that bruises if you look at it wrong,
that heals anyway, stubborn,
stitching itself back together
in the dark while we sleep.

Blessed be weakness—
the knees that give out on the stairs,
the hands that shake pouring coffee,
the heart that skips and startles us
into remembering we are alive.

And blessed, above all, be the voice
that answers when we call in the middle of the night,
not because it has an answer,
not because it can fix what is broken,
but because it says *I'm here*,
and means it,
and stays on the line
until the shaking stops,
until the dark loosens its grip
just enough
for morning.

---

*This poem inhabits a strange and necessary territory: it refuses the traditional shape of blessing, which usually moves toward the beautiful, the whole, the deserving. Instead, it insists that sacredness is not reserved for what is clean or complete. By blessing the thief alongside the mother, the debt alongside the gift, the failing body alongside its stubborn healing, the poem argues that reverence must widen to hold all of human experience—including what we are taught to be ashamed of. The final image, of a voice answering a call for help, grounds this expansive theology in something intimate and small: not a cosmic redemption, but the simple, world-altering fact that someone picks up the phone. In this way, the poem transforms blessing from a hierarchy of the sacred and profane into an ethic of attention—a way of saying that everything broken is still, somehow, holy.*
outputs.L5:
# Blessed Days

Monday often arrives with a groan, carrying the weight of a fresh work week and the end of weekend freedom. Yet there's something to bless even in this challenging start—a new beginning, a clean slate, an opportunity to set intentions for the days ahead. To bless Monday is to acknowledge that even difficult transitions can hold hidden gifts.

Tuesday, by contrast, often feels like the quiet workhorse of the week. It lacks the dramatic reputation of Monday or the anticipatory joy of Friday, yet it deserves its own blessing too. Tuesday is where routines settle in, where the initial resistance of Monday fades into productive rhythm. It's a day of steady progress, often overlooked but essential.

To bless both Monday and Tuesday is to practice gratitude for the ordinary days—the ones that don't announce themselves with celebration or relief, but simply ask us to show up. There's wisdom in blessing not just the days we love, but every day that structures our lives. Each day, whether Monday's fresh start or Tuesday's steady continuation, offers its own quiet gift: another chance to work, to connect, to grow, and to move forward.

Perhaps the real blessing is this: recognizing that every day of the week, however mundane, contributes to the fullness of a life well-lived. Monday teaches us renewal. Tuesday teaches us persistence. Together, they remind us that blessings aren't reserved for extraordinary moments alone—they're woven into the fabric of everyday time.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse "blessing" poem that repeats the word "bless" throughout, moving between humor, grief, and tenderness.
counterfactuals.output:
**Blessing for the Ordinary Wreckage**

Bless the coffee that went cold
while I was busy grieving something smaller than a person—
a sock, a Tuesday, the years I thought
would feel different than this.

Bless my mother's hands, spotted now
like the undersides of leaves in October,
still reaching for my face
like I am something she invented
and isn't sure she got right.

Bless the dog who died in July
and the dog who is dying now, slower,
so that I have time to practice
a grief I already know the shape of,
the way you learn a language
by loving someone who speaks it.

Bless the joke that fell flat at the funeral—
someone had to say something
and I said the wrong thing
and my aunt laughed anyway, wetly,
which might be its own kind of blessing,
laughter breaking like a fever.

Bless the body for staying,
for the knees that ache like an argument
you keep having with the stairs,
for the heart doing its one blunt job
over and over, dumbly faithful,
a dog that doesn't know
its owner is never coming back
and waits by the door regardless.

Bless the door.
Bless the waiting.

Bless my father's voice on the answering machine
that I have not deleted in six years,
though he has been gone for five,
because bless the machines
that let the dead keep talking
in their ordinary, unbearable way—
*just calling to say hello, call me back
when you get a chance, no rush.*

No rush.

Bless the rush anyway, the traffic,
the late fee, the burnt toast,
the small catastrophes
that let me feel something
that isn't the big one.

Bless the big one too, I guess.
Bless it through my teeth.

Bless whoever invented casseroles
for the grieving, foil-wrapped and nameless,
appearing on porches like small moons.
Bless the porch. Bless the moon.
Bless the woman two doors down
who brought soup and stayed too long
and talked about her divorce
because grief doesn't know
whose grief it's supposed to be.

Bless the awkward hug,
the hand that doesn't know
where to land on your back,
patting like it's trying to burp a very large,
very sad baby. Bless the baby.
Bless the very sadness of it, comic
in its heaviness, the way all the biggest things
are secretly a little ridiculous—
love, and dying, and the human need
to bring a casserole to both.

Bless the years I'll forget this,
distracted by something as small
as a good song on the radio,
sun on the kitchen floor,
the particular blue of an ordinary Tuesday
that will not, this time, be about grief at all.

Bless that forgetting too.
Let it be a mercy
and not a failure of the heart
to hold what it loved.

Bless the failure of the heart to hold
everything at once—
bless its smallness,
its ridiculous, insistent smallness,
still doing its one blunt job,
bless, bless, bless
like a stutter, like a prayer
that doesn't know how to end
so it just keeps beginning.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a poem in the style of a litany, blessing small everyday things as well as painful memories?
counterfactuals.output:
# A Litany for What Remains

Blessed be the chipped mug that still holds the coffee,
the handle worn smooth by a decade of mornings.

Blessed be the socks that never match,
the drawer that sticks, the door that knows your shoulder's weight.

Blessed be the voicemail I cannot delete,
her voice still asking if I've eaten, still certain that I haven't.

Blessed be the grocery list in handwriting not my own,
found folded in a coat I meant to donate.

Blessed be the silence after the diagnosis,
the way the clock kept ticking like nothing had been said.

Blessed be the porch light left on for people who aren't coming home,
and blessed be the moths who don't know the difference.

Blessed be the scar that aches before the rain,
teaching my body to read the sky.

Blessed be the empty chair at the table,
still pulled out, still waiting, still setting a place in the shape of absence.

Blessed be the songs that ambush me in grocery stores,
that turn cereal aisles into chapels.

Blessed be the photographs going soft at the edges,
blessed be forgetting, and blessed be remembering wrong.

Blessed be the anger that finally quieted into something softer,
though I miss its heat some days.

Blessed be the small kindness of strangers—
the held door, the correct change, the "after you."

Blessed be the nights I could not sleep,
and the mornings that arrived anyway, indifferent and holy.

Blessed be this body, this rented house of grief and gladness,
still standing, still opening its eyes.

Blessed be the ordinary Tuesday,
which asks nothing of us but to continue.

Blessed be it all—
the mended and the broken,
the folded laundry and the unfolded grief,
the last light through the kitchen window,
calling everything home.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal, emotionally raw poem about riding the subway, student debt, and grief, using anaphora with the word "bless."
counterfactuals.output:
**Bless the 6 Train at 2 AM**

Bless the fluorescent flicker that makes everyone
look like they're already ghosts, already
practicing for the part.

Bless the interest that compounds like grief does—
quietly, at night, while you're pretending to sleep,
turning small numbers into cathedrals
you'll never stop paying for.

Bless the stranger's shoulder I fell asleep on
because it smelled like my father's coat
the year before the year he died,
and I let myself believe, for four stops,
that grief was just a transfer I hadn't made yet.

Bless the automated voice that says *stand clear*
as if anything in this life
has ever given us that option.

Bless the loan officer's email, subject line
*URGENT: Payment Due*, sitting unread
next to the one from the hospital
that I also cannot open,
both of them asking the same question:
*what do you owe, and to whom, and for how long.*

Bless the way the tunnel goes dark
between stations, that small practice-death,
that rehearsal in becoming nothing,
before the light finds you again
whether you wanted it to or not.

Bless my mother's voice on the phone saying
*just take the next test, baby, it'll be worth it,*
not knowing yet that worth
is a station some trains don't stop at anymore.

Bless the diploma in a drawer
next to his obituary,
two pieces of paper
that cost me everything
and prove nothing.

Bless the ads for debt relief
plastered beside the ads for the show
about people who start over,
as if starting over
were a thing you could buy a ticket for,
as if the doors ever really open
before they close.

Bless the swipe that doesn't work,
the *please swipe again* that sounds,
some nights, like the last thing
anyone will ever say to me—
kind, mechanical, unmoved,
asking me to try again
what already broke me.

Bless this whole underground country
of the almost-late, the still-owing, the recently-orphaned,
riding in the dark together,
none of us looking at each other,
all of us
being carried
somewhere.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a prose-poem that blesses ordinary objects and people (like train commuters, hair, loans, friends) in an unconventional, stream-of-consciousness way.
counterfactuals.output:
# Blessing for the Unremarkable

Blessed be the 7:42 train and everyone on it pretending not to cry, the woman with her forehead against glass watching telephone poles count out her life in even measures, blessed be the man who gives up his seat without being asked, blessed be his tired knees.

Blessed be hair — the way it forgets us, falls in the shower drain like small confessions, the gray hairs that arrive uninvited and stay anyway, stubborn as old friends. Blessed be the friend who calls at 11pm not to talk but just to breathe on the phone with you, blessed be that silence, fuller than words.

Blessed be loans — yes, even loans, the quiet arithmetic of hope, the signature that says *I believe I will still be here in twelve years*, blessed be the interest that grows like something almost alive, blessed be whoever invented "minimum payment," a phrase soft as forgiveness.

Blessed be the coffee cup left with lipstick on the rim, blessed be the person who didn't wash it yet, who is somewhere else entirely, laughing maybe, or asleep. Blessed be sleep, that small daily death we agree to nightly, trusting we'll be handed back our names in the morning.

Blessed be the umbrella that turns inside out in wind, comic and useless and trying anyway. Blessed be trying anyway.

Blessed be the group chat that goes quiet for months then erupts over a meme, blessed be the friends who don't perform friendship, who let it sit in a drawer like a photograph, still developing, still becoming itself.

Blessed be the body, that old rented apartment, blessed be its creaks and its refusal to be finished, blessed be the socks that never find their pairs — somewhere there is a museum of missing socks and I hope it's warm there, I hope they're happy.

Blessed be waiting rooms and their old magazines, blessed be the receptionist who says "he'll see you now" like a small mercy.

Blessed be all of it — the ordinary miracle of getting up again, the loans and hairbrushes and creased photographs, the friends who become family without paperwork, the trains that keep arriving, faithful as forgiveness, carrying us toward whatever we've decided to call *home.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem that mixes tenderness and dark humor, structured like a benediction, touching on love, illness, and city life.
counterfactuals.output:
# Benediction for the Weary and In Love

Blessed be the pharmacist who knows your name
and doesn't ask why you're back again so soon,
who slides the paper bag across the counter
like communion, like he's seen worse, like he cares
in that tired municipal way of someone
who has held everyone's chemical sadness
in his latex-gloved hands.

Blessed be your body, that traitor, that old dog
that still comes when called most days,
that carries you up four flights without elevator
to the apartment where I am waiting
with soup that is mostly broth and good intentions.

May the subway doors open for you specifically.
May they not close on your bag, your coat, your faith in public transit.
May the stranger who coughs on you at rush hour
find enlightenment, or at least some cough drops.

Bless the illness that taught us to say I love you
in the smaller hours, between the fever checks,
between the "how do you feel" and the "still here, still here."
Bless the couch that became our country,
its cushions worn to the shape of our surrender.

Blessed be the city that doesn't care about either of us,
its indifference a kind of tenderness—
no one asking you to be brave here,
no one clocking how thin you've gotten,
just the bodega cat, ancient and unimpressed,
blinking at your grief like it's weather.

May your test results be boring.
May your doctor have good bedside manner
or at least decent handwriting.
May the good days outnumber the bad
by a margin that makes the math worth doing.

And when the night comes, as it does, relentless landlord
demanding its rent of worry—
may I be there to hold your hand
like it's the only prayer I know,
because it is, because you are,
because in this small kitchen, this rented life,
this body that keeps almost failing you—

I have found something worth blessing.
Even now. Especially now.
Amen, or whatever we call it
when it's just us, just this,
just love refusing to be reasonable
in a world that gives it every reason to leave.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
